summary.text: Kevin Parker is the incumbent Democratic state senator for District 21 in Brooklyn, in office since 2003. A longtime Flatbush resident, he worked in state and city government and taught at Brooklyn College before his election. He chairs the Senate Energy and Telecommunications Committee, previously served as Majority Whip, ran unsuccessfully for New York City Comptroller in 2025, and is seeking re-election.

paragraphs.text: A lifelong Brooklyn resident who has lived in Flatbush for more than 31 years, according to his official Senate biography; attended New York City public schools including Midwood High School.

Earned a B.S. in public service from Pennsylvania State University (1989) and an M.S. from the New School for Social Research (1993); has been pursuing a Ph.D. in political science at the CUNY Graduate School and University Center.

Worked as a project manager for the New York State Urban Development Corporation, an instructor at Brooklyn College (1993-1997), a political action director for Paine Webber (1998-1999), and a special assistant in the Office of the New York State Comptroller (2000-2002).

Served as a legislative aide to New York City Council Member Una Clarke and as special assistant to Assemblyman Nick Perry; also worked as a special assistant to Manhattan Borough President Ruth Messinger and was a New York City Urban Fellow.
Ran for New York City Council in 2001 but was not elected, then won the State Senate seat and took office in 2003.

Chairs the Senate Energy and Telecommunications Committee; also a member of the Banks, Civil Service and Pensions, Finance, Health, Internet and Technology, Judiciary, and Rules committees. Previously served as Senate Majority Whip.

According to his official bio, he founded the New York Ready Emergency Preparedness Unit, is First Vice Chair of the Association of Black, Puerto Rican & Asian Legislators, and was named a 2026 New York State Senate Veterans' Hall of Fame honoree.
Ran in the 2025 Democratic primary for New York City Comptroller and was eliminated in round 2 of the ranked-choice tabulation; Mark Levine won the general election.
